3.7 Financial Statement Analysis

The three statements

Section titled “The three statements”

To value a stock, you first need to read the company’s financial statements. US public companies file a 10-Q report each quarter and a 10-K report each year, with financial statements prepared under US Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP). Three statements matter most.

The balance sheet lists, at a point in time, what the company owns (assets AAA), what it owes others (liabilities LLL), and what is left for shareholders (shareholders’ equity EEE):

A=L+EA = L + EA=L+E

Assets include cash, receivables, inventory, plant and equipment; liabilities include payables, loans and bonds; equity consists mainly of capital paid in by shareholders and the profits kept in the company over the years (retained earnings).

The income statement records revenue and expenses over a period (a quarter or a year). Here is a simplified example:

ItemAmount
Revenue1,000
Less: cost of goods sold600
Gross profit400
Less: selling, general, administrative and R&D expenses200
Less: depreciation50
Operating income (EBIT)150
Less: interest30
Pretax income120
Less: income tax (rate 21%)25.2
Net income94.8

The income statement follows accrual accounting: revenue is recognized when goods or services are delivered, even if the customer has not paid yet; expenses are recognized in the same period as the related revenue, even if the cash was paid long ago or has not been paid yet. For example, a company that spends 500 on a machine that lasts 10 years does not count all 500 as an expense in the year of purchase; it recognizes 50 of depreciation each year. Depreciation is an expense, but not a cash payment in that year.

Accounting profit differs from economic profit: it deducts the interest on borrowing but not the opportunity cost of shareholders’ capital (cost of capital).

The cash flow statement records the cash actually received and paid over a period, in three groups:

  • operating activities: cash received and paid in daily operations;
  • investing activities: buying and selling plant and equipment, acquiring other companies, buying and selling investments;
  • financing activities: borrowing and repaying, issuing and buying back shares, paying dividends.
Check C1
At the start of the year a company borrows 50 to buy equipment that lasts 5 years (ignore taxes and interest). On the day of the purchase, what changes on the income statement?
The equipment lasts 5 years. Under accrual accounting, is its cost expensed all at once when it is bought?
Neither borrowing nor buying equipment is a sale, so neither creates revenue.
Depreciation is recognized year by year while the equipment is used; on the day of purchase it has not been used yet.

How the statements link

Section titled “How the statements link”

The three statements are different views of the same transactions, and they are tied together exactly:

  • Net income increases equity: ending retained earnings = beginning retained earnings + net income − dividends.
  • The total of the three groups of cash flows equals the change in cash on the balance sheet.
  • Operating cash flow can be derived from net income (the indirect method): add back depreciation and other expenses that use no cash, then subtract the increase in working capital. Working capital is mainly receivables plus inventory minus payables: higher receivables mean part of revenue has not yet been received in cash; higher inventory means cash was paid for goods not yet sold; higher payables mean part of the expenses has not yet been paid in cash.
CFO=NI+Dep−ΔWC\text{CFO} = \text{NI} + \text{Dep} - \Delta \text{WC}CFO=NI+Dep−ΔWC

Here CFO is operating cash flow, NI is net income, Dep is depreciation, and ΔWC\Delta \text{WC}ΔWC is the increase in working capital.

So profit and cash flow can differ a lot. Figure 2-1 looks at a company whose revenue grows.

Check C2
In Figure 2-1, keep days of receivables at 60 and raise revenue growth from 0 to 40%. Compared with five-year total net income, five-year total operating cash flow:
The faster the growth, the more new receivables each year: revenue already recognized but not yet received in cash.
The two are equal only if receivables stay constant. What happens to receivables when revenue grows?
Do rising receivables put cash flow below profit or above it?

Earnings quality

Section titled “Earnings quality”

Accrual accounting makes profit a better measure of a period’s results, but it also requires many estimates and judgments: how many years a machine will last, how much of the receivables will never be collected, whether inventory has lost value, how much revenue of a multi-year contract to recognize in each period. When the estimates are reasonable, profit reflects the business better than cash flow; when they are too optimistic, profit is overstated.

How far reported earnings reflect lasting results of the business that eventually turn into cash is earnings quality. Common checks are:

  • Compare net income with operating cash flow: over the long run they should be close; if profit stays well above cash flow, find out why.
  • See whether receivables and inventory grow much faster than revenue.
  • Look at changes in accounting estimates and policies and their effect on profit (explained in the notes to the annual report).
  • Separate lasting profit from one-time items (gains on asset sales, legal settlements and so on).

Not every number on the income statement is equally “hard”. How does a small change in an accounting estimate affect profit and cash flow? Check C3 looks at an example.

Check C3
A company lengthens the depreciation life of its servers from 4 to 6 years (ignore taxes). This raises operating income, and operating cash flow rises by the same amount.
Think: is depreciation a cash payment? Does changing the depreciation life change the cash the company actually pays?

Common ways of dressing up earnings

Section titled “Common ways of dressing up earnings”

Managers’ pay and reputation are often tied to reported profit, another example of the principal-agent problem. Common ways of dressing up earnings include:

  • Recognizing revenue early: for example, shipping large amounts to distributors at the end of a quarter (channel stuffing), so revenue rises and receivables rise even faster.
  • Capitalizing expenses: recording spending that should be a current expense as an asset and spreading it over later years, which raises current profit.
  • Adjusting estimates: lengthening the useful lives of assets, cutting allowances for bad debts, or setting aside large reserves in good years and releasing them in bad years (“cookie jar” reserves).
  • Recurring “one-time” charges: restructuring charges that appear every year, with investors asked every year to ignore them.
  • Stressing “adjusted” earnings: besides GAAP earnings, companies often report non-GAAP earnings that exclude stock-based compensation, amortization, restructuring charges and other items; adjusted earnings are often well above GAAP earnings.

Most of these practices are legal, and some have good reasons, but they widen the gap between profit and cash flow and reverse in later years. In analysis, go back to cash flow and read the notes to the annual report.

Check C4
A company stresses "adjusted earnings" that exclude stock-based compensation (pay to employees in shares or options). Why is stock-based compensation still a real cost for existing shareholders?
When pay is given in shares, the company pays no cash in the period.
Stock-based compensation is generally deducted as an expense before tax; it does not raise the company's tax.
Employees' work has value; without shares, the company would pay cash. What do new shares issued to employees mean for existing shareholders?

Summary

Section titled “Summary”
  • Balance sheet: assets = liabilities + equity; income statement: revenue, expenses and net income over a period; cash flow statement: cash from operating, investing and financing activities.
  • Accrual accounting recognizes revenue at delivery and matches expenses to revenue; depreciation spreads the cost of a long-lived asset over its life and is not a cash payment in the period.
  • Net income flows into retained earnings; the three groups of cash flows add up to the change in cash; operating cash flow = net income + depreciation − increase in working capital.
  • Earnings quality asks how far profit is lasting and turns into cash; compare profit with cash flow, and watch for changes in estimates, one-time items and “adjusted” earnings.

Exercises

Section titled “Exercises”
Question 1 ★
This year a company has net income of 80 and depreciation of 30; receivables rose by 25, inventory by 15 and payables by 5.
(a) Use the indirect method to find operating cash flow.
(b) Capital spending (buying equipment) this year is 60, and the company paid 40 in dividends. What is operating cash flow minus capital spending? Where might the dividend money come from? Can this last?
Question 2
(a) A company starts the year with equity of 500. This year net income is 120, it pays dividends of 30 and spends 50 in cash buying back shares, with no new shares issued. What is equity at year end?
(b) Another company with steady profits has for years spent more on buybacks than its net income, and the equity on its balance sheet has become negative. Does this mean it is insolvent and about to go bankrupt?
Question 3
A company's revenue grew from 1000 to 1200 (20%), and year-end receivables rose from 100 to 160.
(a) How did days of receivables (receivables ÷ revenue × 365) change?
(b) Give one harmless explanation and one worrying explanation. What other information should you check to tell them apart?
Question 4
Define the accruals ratio = (net income − operating cash flow) ÷ total assets. Companies A and B each have total assets of 1000 and net income of 100; A's operating cash flow is 120 and B's is 40.
(a) What is each company's accruals ratio?
(b) Research (Sloan, 1996) found that companies with high accruals ratios tend to have falling profits and lower stock returns later. Why are profits made of accruals harder to sustain than profits made of cash? Why might the market not fully reflect this?
